final_proof:
Put \(H=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-,-)\) and \(K=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-,G-)\), regarded as functors \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}\). Thus, on objects,
\[
H(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD,C),\qquad K(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D,GC).
\]
A morphism \(f^{\mathrm{op}}:D_1^{\mathrm{op}}\to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}\) in \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\) corresponds to a morphism \(f:D_2\to D_1\) in \(\mathbf D\). Hence, for a morphism \((f^{\mathrm{op}},g):(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)\to(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)\) of the product category, where \(g:C_1\to C_2\), the two functors act by
\[
H(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)(h)=g\circ h\circ Ff,\qquad K(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)(k)=Gg\circ k\circ f.
\]
These expressions are well typed: \(Ff:FD_2\to FD_1\), so the first sends \(FD_1\to C_1\) to \(FD_2\to C_2\), and the second similarly sends \(D_1\to GC_1\) to \(D_2\to GC_2\).

Suppose first that Definition 1 holds. A natural isomorphism \(\alpha:H\to K\) has, at every object \((D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\), a component
\[
\alpha_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD,C)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D,GC).
\]
Because \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism, this component is an isomorphism in \(\mathbf{Set}\), hence a bijection. Moreover, naturality at \((f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\) says
\[
K(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}=\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}\circ H(f^{\mathrm{op}},g).
\]
After substituting the displayed formulas for \(H\) and \(K\), this is precisely the commutativity condition in Definition 2 (with its two sides written in the opposite order). Thus Definition 2 holds.

Conversely, suppose Definition 2 holds. Its assigned bijections form a family of maps \(\alpha_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)}:H(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\to K(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\). Every morphism in \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C\) is a pair \((f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\), and the equation required in Definition 2 is exactly
\[
K(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}=\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}\circ H(f^{\mathrm{op}},g).
\]
Therefore the family \(\alpha\) is a natural transformation \(H\to K\). It remains only to verify that it is a natural isomorphism, rather than merely an objectwise bijective natural transformation. For each object \(X=(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\), let \(\beta_X=\alpha_X^{-1}\). If \(u:X\to Y\) is any morphism of the product category, naturality of \(\alpha\) gives
\[
K(u)\circ\alpha_X=\alpha_Y\circ H(u).
\]
Composing on the left with \(\beta_Y\) and on the right with \(\beta_X\) yields
\[
\beta_Y\circ K(u)=H(u)\circ\beta_X,
\]
which is the naturality condition for \(\beta:K\to H\). Componentwise, \(\beta_X\alpha_X=\mathrm{id}_{H(X)}\) and \(\alpha_X\beta_X=\mathrm{id}_{K(X)}\); hence \(\beta\) is a two-sided natural inverse of \(\alpha\). Thus \(\alpha\) is a natural isomorphism, and Definition 1 holds. The two definitions are therefore equivalent.
